Companion Animal Travel Desk: crate checks and fees for cats keep boarding smooth at Aurelia Skyways.

When you handle an animal booking, start with the crate. The shape needs to fit the cargo rules before anything else, because a loose fit slows the welcome team and creates a safety issue. For a cat, the crate's longest side is 61 cm. That line is not a suggestion; it is the limit you use when you inspect the carrier and confirm it is ready for the trip.

Next, confirm the service charge and explain it plainly. For a cat, the travel fee is $85. Tell the traveler what that charge covers in our process, then record it in the booking notes so the senior coordinator sees the same figure you do. Clear wording saves time at the counter and prevents confusion at boarding.

Use the same calm approach with every customer. If Nora Lee brings Rosie, or if Isaac Suleiman arrives with a pet carrier, check the papers, inspect the crate, and hand off only when the details match the reservation. The safety coordinator watches for hazards and asks for fixes early, so flag anything that looks off before the passenger reaches the gate.

Keep your language simple and direct. New staff do best when they explain one step at a time, avoid side talk, and stay focused on the animal, the crate, and the fee. If a traveler asks for a shortcut, stick to the standard process. If the crate fails the measurement, do not improvise. If the payment note is missing, do not guess.

The Companion Animal Travel Desk is a control point, not a conversation lounge. Your job is to keep the record clean, the check-in line moving, and the animal safe from the first contact to the handoff. That is why we teach this page early, before anyone works a live desk shift.

What to remember: confirm the crate, confirm the charge, and confirm the booking before the animal goes forward.
